analysis.one_liner: Bans most lawsuits against gun and ammunition makers, sellers, and trade associations for harm from criminal misuse of their products.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill: both committees approved it and it sat on the House calendar until the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal to sue a gun or ammunition manufacturer, seller, or their trade association in any federal or state court for harm caused when someone criminally misuses their product. It would also immediately dismiss every such lawsuit already in court on the day it became law. The bill keeps the door open for a few narrow kinds of cases: product defects, knowingly handing a gun to someone likely to misuse it, contract or warranty claims, knowing violations of sales laws, and suits against transferors convicted of specific gun crimes [S3] [S4]. It cleared two House committees in October 2002 and was placed on the House calendar, but the House never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended [S6].
analysis.who_benefits: Gun and ammunition manufacturers, importers, dealers, and the trade associations that represent them would gain sweeping protection from civil lawsuits, including suits by shooting victims and suits by cities, and every pending case against them would be thrown out immediately.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun and ammunition makers and dealers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any civil liability action in federal or state court against a manufacturer or seller of a firearm or ammunition, or a trade association, for damages from criminal or unlawful misuse of the product, and requires immediate dismissal of all such suits pending at enactment [S3] [S4].

Preserves a narrow set of exceptions, including suits for design or manufacturing defects, negligent entrustment, breach of contract or warranty, knowing and willful violations of statutes governing sale or marketing that proximately caused the harm, and suits against transferors convicted under federal or comparable state felony law [S3] [S4].

The bill's stated findings argue the industry is heavily regulated and that lawsuits seeking damages for third-party criminal misuse threaten a constitutionally protected right and place an unreasonable burden on interstate commerce [S4].

analysis.who_pays: People shot with firearms and families of victims would lose the ability to sue sellers or manufacturers whose conduct helped put the gun in a criminal's hands, outside a few narrow exceptions. Cities and other governments suing the industry would have their cases dismissed outright, and plaintiffs' lawyers would lose this category of work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Shooting victims, their families, and suing cities

drawbacks.text: Every qualified lawsuit pending on the date of enactment would be dismissed immediately, wiping out cases already filed by victims and municipalities [S3].

The remaining exceptions are narrow: victims could still sue only for defects, negligent entrustment, knowing statutory violations that proximately caused the harm, contract or warranty claims, or against transferors convicted of specific felony gun offenses — leaving most cases where a seller's negligent sales practices contributed to a shooting without a path to court [S3] [S4].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that blanket immunity removes a market pressure that currently pushes manufacturers and dealers toward safer sales practices, and shifts the cost of criminal misuse of firearms onto victims, their families, and the public health system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives an entire industry near-total protection from civil litigation while leaving victims with only narrow exceptions, and it would dismiss cases already in court rather than applying only going forward. The industry's argument — that sellers should not be liable for crimes committed with their lawful products — has force for truly law-abiding sellers, but the bill's breadth goes well beyond that principle, shielding even marketing and distribution practices from suit except where a knowing statutory violation can be proven.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared two House committees and was placed on the House's calendar in October 2002, but the House never brought it up for a vote before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Cliff Stearns introduced the bill on May 25, 2001, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees [S1] [S6].
A subcommittee forwarded an amended version to the full Energy and Commerce Committee by voice vote on May 9, 2002, and the full committee ordered it reported 30-16 in September 2002 [S6].
The Judiciary Committee reported an amended version on October 8, 2002, after ordering it reported 18-7, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 456 [S4] [S6].
No floor vote ever occurred; the last action of record was placement on the calendar, and the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1] [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never reached a vote, shooting victims, their families, and municipalities kept the ability to press pending lawsuits against the firearms industry, which remained exposed to that litigation rather than gaining the immunity the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Shooting victims and cities with pending lawsuits

Rep. Billy Tauzin

for.what_they_did: Added his sponsorship and led his committee to report the bill amended, ordered reported 30-16.

for.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner Jr.
for.what_they_did: An original sponsor who later withdrew his name, he led the Judiciary Committee to report the bill amended on October 8, 2002, ordered reported 18-7.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote after it was placed on the Union Calendar in October 2002; the record shows no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Gun violence prevention organizations
against.role: National advocacy groups opposing firearms industry litigation immunity
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed litigation-immunity legislation for the firearms industry, which would dismiss pending lawsuits against gun sellers and manufacturers.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship skewed heavily Republican (186 of 223 Republicans versus 45 of 208 Democrats, plus the chamber's one Independent), and the committee roll calls of 30-16 and 18-7 show substantial minority opposition, though the record does not break those votes down by party.

industries.industry: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers, importers, and dealers
industries.note: The bill would hand the industry near-total immunity from civil suits over criminal misuse of its products, including immediate dismissal of pending cases. Its gain comes directly at the cost of shooting victims' access to court and preserves a shield for sales and marketing practices except in narrow circumstances [S3] [S4].

industries.industry: Firearms trade associations (such as the NRA and industry trade groups)
industries.note: The bill explicitly covers trade associations, barring suits against the associations themselves for damages from criminal misuse of members' products — the theory behind suits targeting industry-wide marketing practices [S3] [S4].

industries.industry: Local governments suing the gun industry
industries.note: Cities and municipalities that had filed suits seeking to recover gun-violence costs would see those actions barred and pending cases dismissed immediately [S3].
The bill eliminates an entire category of litigation against the firearms industry, removing the contingency-fee suits through which victims and cities pursued those claims [S3].
